qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

It seems we have got used to Erdoğan’s changes of direction: first he’s attacking the German chancellor in Berlin, and the week after, he’s playing the nice guy towards the Greek Prime Minister in Athens. However, his climb-down is no accident. Erdoğan is teetering on a tightrope between the EU, NATO, the USA and Israel. He has unfinished business with Syria, Iraq, Libya, and Armenia, so he wants to show that he has turned over a new leaf. His aim is to win favourable treatment from Europe and the USA and get the fighter jets he needs. If his efforts to acquire F16s are unsuccessful, he’ll try his luck with a European fighter jet, the Eurofighter. So far, we have seen a positive attitude in Spain and the UK, while Germany has certain objections and Italy has not adopted a position. Everyone knows these fighter jets could potentially be used to threaten Cyprus and Greece. In view of this: 1.
What action is the Commission taking to ensure a common stance among the Member States that are co-producers of Eurofighter?
Is it assessing the risks entailed in the sale to third countries of military equipment that could be used against EU Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.3.2024) The EU has expressed concern about Türkiye’s actions and urged Türkiye to stop all threats and actions that damage good neighbourly relations, and to respect the sovereignty of all Member States over their territorial sea and airspace1. The EU welcomes the marked improvement in relations between Greece and Türkiye since early 20232. The control on the export and transit of arms by Member States is subject to national legislation, the Council Common Position (CP) 2008/944/CFSP3 and the Arms Trade Treaty4. Under Article 2(5)(b) of the CP, Member States, while assessing export license application, take into account the risk of use of the items concerned against their forces or those of other Member States. Final decision is taken by Member States. This also includes potential export of the Eurofighter, subject to unanimous approval of all project participants. The Commission has no mandate in relation to coordination of Member States position regarding their arms exports. Member States continuously work in the Common Foreign and Security Policy framework to promote convergence in arms exports, inter alia, by exchanging relevant information. The Council’s Working Party on Conventional Arms Export remains seized of the matter of arms exports to Türkiye. In the Council Conclusions of 14 October 20195, the EU recalled the decision taken by some Member States to halt arms exports to Türkiye, and Member States committed to strong national positions on the basis of the CP, including strict application of its criterion 4 on regional stability as potential basis for license denial, but did not impose arms embargo. There have been no further initiatives of Member States since 2019 aiming to further restrict arms exports to Türkiye.
